framework: Asking the Right Questions: A Guide to Critical Thinking
key_work: Asking the Right Questions: A Guide to Critical Thinking (1st ed. 1981, 12th ed. 2019)
description: Browne and Keeley's framework consists of 10 sequential questions that form a complete protocol for analyzing any argument or persuasive text. The genius of the framework is its sequenced diagnostic logic: each question reveals a different potential failure mode, and applying all 10 ensures comprehensive critical analysis.
dewey_connection: The Browne-Keeley sequence maps directly to Dewey's reflective thinking: beginning with framing (questions 1-2), proceeding through analysis (3-8), and arriving at integrative judgment (9-10). The emphasis on 'right questions' echoes Dewey's insistence that the quality of inquiry depends on the quality of the questions it addresses.
paul_elder_connection: Questions 1-2 map to Purpose and Question-at-Issue; 3-5 to Concepts and Assumptions; 6-7 to Information and Inference; 8-10 to Implications and Point of View.

ten_questions.question: What are the issue and the conclusion?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify the focal point of the argument before any evaluation can proceed. Without clear identification of the conclusion, analysis has no target.

issue_types.description: Concerns what is, was, or will be true — empirically resolvable in principle
Concerns what should be, what is right, what is valuable — requires value judgments

diagnostic_questions: What is the author trying to persuade me to believe or do?
If I was to summarize this argument in one sentence, what would I say?
Is this issue descriptive or prescriptive?
failure_modes: Confusing the issue with the conclusion
Failing to distinguish prescriptive from descriptive claims

ten_questions.question: What are the reasons?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify the explicit and implicit reasons (premises) offered in support of the conclusion. Reasons are what the author wants us to accept as grounds for accepting the conclusion.
diagnostic_questions: Why should I believe this conclusion?
What reasons are explicitly stated?
Are there unstated reasons being assumed?
Can I map the reasoning: 'Because of [reasons], therefore [conclusion]'?
failure_modes: Accepting conclusions without identifying the reasons
Treating repetition of conclusion as a reason

ten_questions.question: Which words or phrases are ambiguous?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify key terms whose vagueness or ambiguity could mask a weak argument or generate false agreement. Different definitions of a key term may make the argument succeed or fail.
diagnostic_questions: What are the key terms in the issue and reasons?
Could any of these terms be interpreted in multiple ways?
Which interpretation makes the argument strongest? Which weakest?
Is the term used consistently throughout the argument?
failure_modes: Equivocation — using a term in two different senses
Emotive language smuggling in value judgments as factual claims

ten_questions.question: What are the value conflicts and assumptions?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify the value assumptions — beliefs about desirable ends and standards of conduct — that the author must hold for the reasoning to proceed. Value assumptions are especially important in prescriptive arguments.
diagnostic_questions: What values does this reasoning implicitly prioritize?
If this conclusion is true, what must the author value?
What are the competing values that someone who disagrees would hold?
Is there an implicit ranking of values embedded in the argument?
failure_modes: Treating one's own value assumptions as universal
Failing to make value conflicts explicit
Disguising prescriptive claims as empirical ones

ten_questions.question: What are the descriptive assumptions?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify the factual assumptions — beliefs about how the world is — that the author takes for granted. Descriptive assumptions are unstated premises treated as obvious but that may be contested.
diagnostic_questions: What must be true for this reason to support this conclusion?
What am I being asked to take on faith?
Are the reasons relevant to the conclusion only if something else is also true?
What implicit beliefs about people, institutions, or causation does this argument depend on?
failure_modes: Accepting background assumptions as obviously true
Failing to distinguish assumptions from established facts
Missing the hidden premises that do the work

ten_questions.question: Are there any fallacies in the reasoning?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify formal and informal fallacies — errors in the logical structure of the reasoning that are disguised as valid arguments.

key_fallacies.description: Attacking the person making the argument rather than the argument itself
Assuming that one event will inevitably lead to a chain of negative events without justification
Citing sources that lack relevant expertise, have conflicts of interest, or are not representative of expert consensus
Presenting only two options when more exist
Using the conclusion (in disguised form) as one of the premises
Misrepresenting an opponent's position to make it easier to attack
Substituting emotional manipulation for logical support

diagnostic_questions: Does the reasoning make illegitimate shortcuts?
Is the author attacking persons rather than arguments?
Is the authority cited relevant and unbiased?
Has the opposing view been accurately represented?

ten_questions.question: How good is the evidence?
ten_questions.purpose: Evaluate the quality of the empirical evidence used to support factual claims. Even valid reasoning fails if the evidence is poor.

evaluation_criteria: Is the analogy being used to prove or illustrate?

diagnostic_questions: What type of evidence is being offered?
Is this the best type of evidence for this claim?
What are the limitations of this evidence?
Could this evidence be interpreted differently?

ten_questions.question: Are there rival causes?
ten_questions.purpose: Determine whether alternative explanations for the evidence exist that would undermine the causal claims of the argument. Correlation does not establish causation.
rival_cause_types: Reverse causation — Y causes X rather than X causes Y
Confounding variable — Z causes both X and Y
Placebo effect — expectation produces the outcome, not the intervention
Post hoc ergo propter hoc — temporal precedence confused with causation
Selection bias — the groups being compared differ in relevant ways
diagnostic_questions: Could this correlation be explained by a third variable?
Could the direction of causation be reversed?
What would a skeptic say is the real explanation for this data?
Has the author controlled for alternative explanations?

ten_questions.question: Are the statistics deceptive?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify ways in which numerical data can mislead even when technically accurate — through selective presentation, inappropriate comparison groups, or misleading framing.

common_deceptions.example: 'Our drug reduces mortality by 50%!' — from 2% to 1% (relative risk vs. absolute risk)
Using mean income when distribution is highly skewed; median tells a different story
'Crime increased 100%!' — from 1 case to 2 cases in a small town
'Interest rates increased 50%' — from 2% to 3% is a 50% increase but only 1 percentage point
Voluntary online surveys over-represent people with strong opinions

diagnostic_questions: What is the base rate being compared against?
What measures of central tendency would show a different picture?
Who is included and excluded from the statistics?
Are these relative or absolute numbers?

ten_questions.question: What significant information is omitted?
ten_questions.purpose: Identify what the argument does NOT say that would significantly affect one's evaluation of it. All arguments present a selected slice of available information; what is left out is as important as what is included.
omission_types: Long-term consequences of the proposed policy
Relevant context that would reframe the issue
The funding source or interests of those making the argument
diagnostic_questions: What would someone who disagrees want me to know that this argument doesn't mention?
What are the costs, risks, or downsides of the proposed conclusion?
What context would change how I evaluate this argument?
If the argument is correct, what else should be true that I could check?

application_protocol.description: The 10 questions are designed to be applied sequentially — each question builds on the previous. Stopping at question 3 without completing the sequence produces an incomplete analysis.

quick_version.description: When time is limited, questions 1, 2, 5, 6, and 10 provide the highest-leverage analysis.
quick_version.rationale: Issue/conclusion, reasons, descriptive assumptions, fallacies, and omitted information cover the most common argument failure modes.

application_protocol.strong_version: Apply all 10 questions in sequence to produce a comprehensive argument evaluation.

app_usage.template_feature: 10 questions as a template for structured argument analysis
app_usage.exercise_feature: Each question generates a distinct exercise type
app_usage.quick_reference: Question bank surfaced during argument evaluation tasks
app_usage.llm_integration: Claude can evaluate user arguments against the 10-question rubric

historical_origin.pedagogical_origins: M. Neil Browne and Stuart Keeley were both professors at Bowling Green State University in Ohio when they developed 'Asking the Right Questions' in the late 1970s. Browne taught economics and Keeley taught psychology, and both had become frustrated with the gap between their students' ability to reproduce disciplinary content and their ability to critically evaluate the arguments they encountered in coursework, media, and professional life. Their framework was explicitly practical: not a philosophical account of what good reasoning requires, but a usable protocol that students without philosophy training could apply to any persuasive text.
historical_origin.rhetorical_tradition: The 10-question framework sits at the intersection of classical rhetoric, informal logic, and consumer advocacy. The concern with value assumptions and descriptive assumptions (Questions 4 and 5) reflects the rhetorical tradition's attention to enthymemes — unstated premises. The concern with evidence quality (Question 7) and alternative explanations (Question 8) reflects the empirical tradition. The concern with practical significance (Question 10) reflects Browne's background in applied social science.
historical_origin.evolution_across_editions: The framework has gone through twelve editions from 1981 to 2019, with each edition refining the question sequence, adding examples from contemporary public discourse, and expanding the chapter on statistical and research design evaluation (Question 7). The core 10-question structure has remained stable across all editions, suggesting that Browne and Keeley identified a genuinely robust set of failure modes in public argumentation that have not become less relevant over time.
historical_origin.practical_vs_philosophical_distinction: The Browne-Keeley framework occupies a distinctive niche in CT education: it is more practically accessible than philosophical frameworks (Paul-Elder, Delphi, Ennis) but more rigorous than popular CT self-help books. Its audience is explicitly the general educated adult encountering persuasive arguments, not the philosophy student studying logic. This accessibility, combined with its genuine rigor, has made it one of the most widely assigned CT texts in undergraduate general education programs.

teaching_applications.overview: The 10 questions provide a complete diagnostic protocol that students can apply immediately to any argument. The pedagogical challenge is teaching the questions in sequence without letting students treat them as a checklist to complete perfunctorily — each question must be genuinely engaged, not just nominally addressed.

sequential_analysis_exercise.description: Have students work through the full 10-question sequence on a single real argument (editorial, advertisement, policy brief). The sequence must be followed in order: each question builds on the previous ones.
implementation: Step 1 (Q1-2): Identify the issue, conclusion type, and explicit reasons before reading further.
Step 2 (Q3): Identify every ambiguous key term and specify its possible meanings.
Step 3 (Q4-5): Identify value assumptions and descriptive assumptions. For each, ask: 'What must the author take for granted for this reason to support this conclusion?'
Step 4 (Q6): Run each reason through a fallacy screen. Name any fallacy specifically.
Step 5 (Q7-8): Evaluate evidence quality and generate alternative explanations.
Step 6 (Q9-10): Identify meaningful omissions and assess practical significance.
sequential_analysis_exercise.discussion_focus: After the exercise: which questions were most often skipped informally? Students typically address Q1-2 and Q6-7 intuitively but skip Q4-5 (assumption hunting) and Q8-9. These are the questions that expose the most hidden weaknesses.

assumptions_workshop.description: Question 4 (Value Assumptions) and Question 5 (Descriptive Assumptions) are the least intuitive questions in the protocol and the ones students most benefit from practicing in isolation before applying within the full sequence.
assumptions_workshop.activity: Present students with 5-10 argument fragments (1-2 sentences each: reason + conclusion). For each: What value must the author hold for this reason to support this conclusion? What empirical belief about how the world works must be assumed? Which of these assumptions would someone who disagrees most contest?
assumptions_workshop.insight_to_draw_out: Most arguments are contested not at the evidence level but at the assumption level. Identifying the assumptions typically reveals the real locus of disagreement.

alternatives_exercise.description: Question 8 (alternative explanations) is the inference-quality checkpoint: can the student recognize that the evidence cited is consistent with explanations other than the one offered?
alternatives_exercise.activity: Present a causal claim and the evidence cited for it. Students must generate at least three alternative explanations that would account for the same evidence, then evaluate which is most plausible and what additional information would distinguish between them.
alternatives_exercise.connection: This is the same as Delphi's Inference sub-skill of 'Conjecturing Alternatives' — the capacity to avoid premature commitment to the first plausible explanation.

protocol_completeness: Did I identify the issue clearly before evaluating the argument, or did I begin evaluating before I was certain what was being argued?
Did I distinguish the type of issue (descriptive vs. prescriptive) — and apply the appropriate evaluative standards for each?
Did I identify the unstated value assumptions in the argument, or did I only examine the explicitly stated reasons?
Did I generate alternative explanations for the evidence cited, or did I accept the author's explanation and proceed?
habitual_omissions: Which of the 10 questions do I habitually skip in informal reading? (Most people skip Q4, Q5, Q8, and Q9.)
When I identify ambiguity (Q3), do I specify which interpretation makes the argument strongest and which weakest — or do I just note that a term is vague?
When I find a fallacy (Q6), can I name it specifically and explain exactly what makes it fallacious, or do I rely on a vague sense that 'something is wrong'?
Do I assess practical significance (Q10), or do I focus entirely on logical structure without asking whether the claimed effect is large enough to matter?
quality_of_engagement: Am I treating the 10 questions as a genuine analytical protocol, or as a checklist I can complete quickly without really engaging each one?
For the arguments that matter most in my life (professional, personal, political), have I ever applied the full 10-question sequence rather than the 2-3 questions that feel most natural?

toulmin_argument_model.description: The Toulmin model provides a structural account of argument (Claim, Data, Warrant, Backing, Qualifier, Rebuttal); Browne-Keeley provides a diagnostic protocol for evaluating arguments. They operate on the same material from different angles. Browne-Keeley's Questions 1-5 map onto Toulmin components: Q1 = Claim, Q2 = Data and Grounds, Q4-5 = Warrant and Backing. Browne-Keeley's Q6-9 provide the evaluation criteria that Toulmin's structural model does not.
toulmin_argument_model.combined_use: Use Toulmin to diagram an argument's structure; use Browne-Keeley's questions to evaluate whether the structure holds up under scrutiny.

walton_argumentation_schemes.description: Walton's argumentation schemes specify which critical questions are appropriate for each type of argument (Appeal to Authority, Argument from Analogy, Practical Reasoning, etc.). Browne-Keeley's Q6 (fallacies) and Q7 (evidence quality) are generic versions of the more targeted critical questions Walton's schemes prescribe. When the argumentation scheme has been identified (Walton), the specific critical questions for that scheme can replace or supplement the generic Browne-Keeley questions.
walton_argumentation_schemes.key_insight: Browne-Keeley's questions work on any argument; Walton's critical questions are more powerful but require first identifying the argument scheme. Browne-Keeley is the general protocol; Walton is the scheme-specific extension.

delphi_consensus.relationship_type: Practical application of formal skill taxonomy
delphi_consensus.description: The Delphi Report's six skills (Interpretation, Analysis, Evaluation, Inference, Explanation, Self-Regulation) map onto the Browne-Keeley 10 questions: Q1-3 = Interpretation; Q2-5 = Analysis; Q6-7 = Evaluation; Q8 = Inference; Q9-10 = Evaluation/Inference. Browne-Keeley operationalizes Delphi's abstract skill definitions into a concrete sequential question protocol that can be applied without formal training in the Delphi framework.
delphi_consensus.key_difference: Delphi is a formal taxonomic framework for defining and measuring CT; Browne-Keeley is a practical protocol for applying CT to real arguments. Use Delphi to understand the intellectual architecture; use Browne-Keeley to act on it.

logical_fallacies_framework.description: Browne-Keeley's Question 6 ('Are there any fallacies in the reasoning?') references a general fallacy screen. The Logical Fallacies framework provides the complete taxonomy of named informal fallacies that Question 6 draws on. Knowing the names, structures, and distinguishing features of specific fallacies transforms Question 6 from a vague 'something seems wrong' check into a precise diagnostic.
logical_fallacies_framework.practical_connection: A student who knows only Browne-Keeley might answer Q6 with 'yes, I think there's a fallacy here but I'm not sure what kind.' A student who also knows the Logical Fallacies taxonomy answers: 'This is an appeal to questionable authority: the source cited has a financial stake in the conclusion and no relevant expertise.'
